blocks.text: The opening vision joins several images of peace: nations come to Zion for divine instruction, disputes between strong nations are settled, weapons become agricultural tools, and households live without fear under vine and fig tree. Micah 4:1-3 closely parallels Isaiah 2:2-4, while Micah extends the vision through verse 5 by linking international peace with secure ordinary life and a commitment to walk in the name of Israel’s God.

Verses 6-10 gather images of vulnerable people—the lame, the driven away, and the afflicted—with Daughter Zion portrayed in labor. Babylon is named as the place to which Zion will go and from which she will be rescued. Scholars disagree about how this reference is dated and how it relates to the book’s eighth-century material, since Micah likely preserves material shaped over a long history of collection. The imagery also invites attention to displacement, communal fracture, and embodied vulnerability rather than treating Zion only as an abstract symbol.

sections.title: Questions Raised by Babylon and Zion

blocks.text: The transformation of swords into farming tools has made Micah’s vision especially enduring in artistic, political, ecclesial, liberationist, and social-justice settings. Its force in this chapter comes from the way instruction, adjudication, disarmament, and freedom from fear are held together rather than treated as separate hopes.

Micah as a whole combines many forms of prophetic speech, including lament, accusation, judgment, instruction, and salvation oracles. This variety helps place the chapter’s movement from promised peace to anguish, exile, rescue, and conflict within a wider book that does not speak in only one register.
